newsitem.title: USA: Worker injuries contribute to Miami fiscal crisis.
newsitem.headline: Worker injuries contribute to Miami fiscal crisis.

text.p: Nearly one in three Miami city workers files a workers' compensation claim against the cash-strapped city every year, contributing to its current fiscal crisis, a newspaper reported Sunday.
Worker's compensation claims cost the city government $9.3 million last year, a large factor in Miami's $68 million budget shortfall, the Miami Herald reported.

Miami's fiscal crisis, uncovered in the wake of a federal corruption probe that targeted top city officials, is so severe that the city's bonds have been downgraded to junk status and some locals are clamoring for Miami to be abolished. Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles last week appointed a panel to oversee the city's recovery.

City workers have claimed workers' compensation for such incidents as: falling out of a chair at the office, breaking a tooth while eating a candy bar, a smack on the nose from a police horse, a bite from a firehouse dog, an allergic reaction to conch salad and stepping on a rusty nail.
Despite evidence of abuse, Miami has been unable to curtail the claims, the Herald reported. The city receives workers' compensation claims at a rate three times that of Dade County.

Miami spent half of what Dade County spent on compensation even though the county has ten times as many workers, the Herald said after a computer analysis of 20,417 workers' compensation cases paid by the city since 1979.
"Obviously there's been abuse to have such a high number of claims," Miami Mayor Joe Carollo told the Herald.

In one instance, the claim of a firefighter who was hurt playing basketball at the firehouse cost taxpayers $212,929. The Herald found sports injuries cost the city $1.37 million, including 109 basketball injuries, 92 weight training, 82 volleyball, 63 jogging, and three playing catch.

In another case, a garbage worker suffered a hernia lifting a garbage can and was out of work for 702 days. At one point she claimed that her injury left her unable to have sex, but she recently delivered a baby, the Herald reported. Her case cost taxpayers $117,425.
